title: One Platform, Many Marketplaces: Multi-Country and Multi-Brand Architecture
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the multi-country-platforms entry in journal-spec.json; the supporting claims and audience are this spec's own. Units added by this conversion: introduction roadmap p05 (the published introduction named neighbouring chapters but not the chapter's own sections), a Trade-offs lead-in p50 that says what the two trade-off tables show, and a conclusion widened from one paragraph to two (p61 synthesis and callback, p62 hand-off).

know: Tenants, global components and configuration; the platform models from the fork per country to the product platform, with the documented record (Adevinta's 2019 rule and Common Platform, eBay Classifieds, OLX, AVIV).

A tenancy model: tenant codes in every identifier, event, log, metric and cost tag; isolation separated from identity; a configuration hierarchy; extension points; release rings; group-urgent change classes; tenant exit paths.
What to share first and the centralization pendulum.

The platform model is decided per capability, and sharing beneath the product keeps the next swing of the pendulum cheap.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a rule that reaches markets unevenly and a brand's objection, the reader names the tenancy controls that apply.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A fraud rule written on Sunday evening protects one country within the hour, reaches a second country three days later with the next deploy of a shared monolith, and never reaches two others or the group's car marketplace, where the same phone number had registered. A brand that already runs four countries on one stack objects to a group configuration service. Using only this chapter: what tenancy model fixes the rule's path, and how do you answer the brand?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A tenant per brand × country with its code in every identifier, event and configuration; fraud and scam rules as a group-urgent change class that bypasses release rings and reaches every tenant at once, split into a group-owned detector and tenant-owned locale packs run in shadow until reviewed; shared trust signals across brands. The configuration service is mandatory only for global components, so the brand keeps its own configuration for its own services and uses the group service where it consumes a group capability.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Sharing a platform across countries and brands without one product; the tenant as a first-class element; configuration over code with a limit; sharing beneath the product, starting with what is uniform and pooled. Then the phishing rule that reached four countries unevenly, concepts, platform models, a tenancy model, Veldmark's Tenancy model v1, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: classifieds engineering and investor sources (Adevinta, eBay Classifieds Group, OLX, Prosus, Marktplaats, Vinted), standards for locales and currencies, EU law, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

audience.who: Group and enterprise architects, platform-engineering leads and engineering directors of multi-country, multi-brand marketplace groups.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are; multi-tenant SaaS and cloud platforms in general; feature flags and staged rollouts.

From earlier chapters: marketplace profiles (marketplace-taxonomy), vertical requirement profiles (vertical-requirements), the listing event envelope with its tenant field, glossed there as one brand in one country (event-driven-listings), statements of reasons under the DSA (trust-and-safety-architecture, marketplace-regulation), the search index topology (search-architecture), the data platform's purpose-bound sharing (data-platform), and ml-platform's shared, per-brand and per-market models.

Veldmark (fictional), its brands Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly and Keybridge, Yardstick, Safe Deal, Common Ground, the architecture advice forum, Ingrid Halvorsen, Daan Visser and Femke, and the failure-pattern names (The Copy-Paste Country, The Forced Fit, Deal-Shaped Architecture, The Category Straitjacket, Billing by Guesswork).
does_not_know: The terms this chapter owns: tenancy model, global component, configuration over code; and tenant in full (brand × country, distinct from brand, market and marketplace profile).

Tenant identity versus tenant isolation and the three isolation tiers (logical, partitioned, dedicated); the tenant register; the configuration hierarchy; extension points; the configure–extend–fork ladder; release rings, tenant-scoped flags and group-urgent change classes; tenant exit paths.

The six platform models and the public record behind them (Adevinta's 2019 rule and Common Platform, eBay Classifieds Group federation and MoVe, OLX's one-repo frontend and Hydra configuration, AVIV, Vinted).
GDPR Chapter V transfer rules as they bear on data residency; BCP 47 locale tags, ISO 4217 currency codes and Unicode CLDR.

thesis.question: How do you share a platform across countries, brands and verticals without forcing them into one product?
thesis.claim: A group should share a platform across countries, brands and verticals by making the tenant (at Veldmark brand × country, ten tenants) a first-class element that every shared capability carries in identifiers, events, configuration, releases, logs and costs; holding market differences that are data as versioned, schema-checked, effective-dated configuration resolved along a hierarchy, putting differences in behavior behind owned extension points and allowing a fork only with an expiry date; releasing in rings from the smallest tenants to the largest while fraud rules, security fixes and legal takedowns reach all tenants at once; documenting an exit path for every tenant of every shared capability; and deciding the platform model capability by capability rather than once for the group, sharing beneath the product and starting with capabilities whose technology is uniform and whose value grows when data is pooled, while product surfaces stay with the brands.
thesis.disputed_by: Either of two common positions: each country or brand forks the codebase and adapts it locally, or the group converges every brand onto one product platform; both treat the platform model as one decision for the whole group rather than one per capability.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this decides the tenant definition, code format, mandatory carriage and exit-path rule once at group level; decides the platform model capability by capability, scoring each on investment, uniformity of technology and value of pooled data and publishing the scores; shares in order infrastructure, the event backbone and data platform, trust signals and identity, media and search, then taxonomy and the commercial core, leaving product surfaces last; requires an expiry date on every approved fork; and watches adoption without mandate, country branches in code, lead time from the first tenant to the last and a yearly separability drill.
thesis.how_why: On 7 March 2027 a phishing rule protected Tradeyard NL within the hour, reached Belgium on 10 March with the next Yardstick deploy, and never reached Poland, Portugal or Motorvane, where the same phone number had an account. Yardstick held about 2,600 branches on the country code and four category trees. Tenancy model v1 (9 June 2027) defined ten brand × country tenants, mandatory tenant codes, partitioned isolation by default, one configuration service for global components, release rings with the three largest tenants last, group-urgent classes for fraud, security and takedowns, and exit paths, because a private-equity owner may sell any tenant. Replayed, the rule split into a group detector and locale packs within a 48-hour shadow window. Adevinta's 2019 rule and the swings at Adevinta and AVIV are the public record.

supporting_claims.claim: The tenant, at a marketplace group usually brand × country, is defined once and carried by every shared capability in its records, events, configuration, releases, logs, cache keys and cost lines; tenant identity is mandatory everywhere, while isolation is chosen per capability with partitioned isolation as the default.

Market differences that are values are held as schema-checked, versioned, effective-dated configuration resolved along a hierarchy; differences in behavior go behind owned extension points; and a fork is allowed only under a decision record with an expiry date (configure, then extend, and only then fork).

Changes reach tenants through release rings, smallest tenants first, and tenant-scoped flags, while named group-urgent change classes (fraud and scam rules, security fixes, legal takedowns) reach every relevant tenant at once.

Every shared capability records which tenant may use which data and documents an exit path for each tenant, because the boundaries between tenants are legal and commercial as well as technical, and any tenant may be sold, closed or moved.

The platform model is decided capability by capability, not once for the group: the public record shows sharing working within a vertical and at lower layers across verticals, while both public attempts at a converged product platform were rowed back.

A group shares first the capabilities whose technology is uniform and whose value grows when data is pooled, leaves product surfaces to the brands, and designs shared layers so that the next swing of the centralization pendulum is cheap.

role.contribution: Decides how every capability of the part is shared across countries and brands, and how the group keeps the ability to undo a sharing decision.

trade-offs, verticals, failure-modes, ca-view, questions: the book's standard judging sections

flow.rationale: The scene comes first because its incident and inventory are the problems the chapter solves. The concepts follow because every later section uses tenant, tenancy model, global component and configuration over code; placed later, the platform models would be compared in words the reader cannot yet separate. The platform models come before the architecture because the record (sharing within a vertical and beneath the product; converged products rowed back) is what justifies designing for global components rather than one product. The architecture then specifies the tenancy model the record points to, and the worked example applies it to the scene's problem; placed before the architecture, the decision record would cite registers, rings and extension points not yet explained. The judging sections apply the whole design, so they come last, with the Chief Architect's sharing order after the trade-offs and vertical differences it draws on.

hook.content: Most marketplace groups grew one country at a time, and every market that was copied must later be changed separately: a group with ten copies of its insertion flow pays for each new rule, regulation and improvement ten times.

bridge.from_reader_world: Architects of multi-country groups know both failures: country copies that multiply every change, and a group platform imposed as one product that local teams route around.
bridge.to_topic: The architecture between those two failures: a shared platform that earns its tenants through contracts, built on a tenancy model, global components and configuration over code.

thesis_statement.text: Make the tenant a first-class element that every shared capability carries; hold market differences that are data as governed configuration, behavior in owned extension points, and forks only with an expiry date; and share beneath the product, starting with what is uniform and pooled, deciding the model capability by capability.

evidence.shows: Shows why forking is rational at each step and costly in sum: the Copy-Paste Country.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: One Rule, Four Countries, Three Days

sections.heading: Concepts: Tenants, Global Components and Configuration

flow.rationale: Tenant terms come first because the tenancy model is defined in them; identity and isolation follow because they qualify what a tenant is in storage and load; the global component then names what is shared across tenants; configuration over code and extension points name how tenant differences are expressed in it. Placed earlier, the global component would have no tenants to serve.

sections.heading: Architecture: A Tenancy Model for a Marketplace Group
sections.controlling_idea: A tenancy model for a marketplace group consists of a layered split of shared and local, a tenant register, a configuration hierarchy, extension points with the configure–extend–fork ladder, release by tenant with group-urgent classes, data boundaries between tenants, and localization beyond translation.

advances_thesis.how: Specifies each element of the tenancy model the thesis calls for.

flow.rationale: The layer model first, because every later element sits in its tenancy services; the register next, because configuration, rings and exit paths read it; the configuration hierarchy before extension points, because extensions start where configuration ends; release by tenant after both, because rings and flags release configuration and code alike. The first four elements say how a tenant's differences are expressed and changed; the last two turn from mechanisms to what tenants may not share: data boundaries (where data may live and which tenant may use it, which needs the register's legal entity and hosting profile) and localization, which applies configuration, extensions and release scope to language and ends on Belgium, the case that tests the tenant definition. Placed before the register, data boundaries would cite legal-entity and hosting attributes not yet introduced; placed in the concepts, localization would have no configuration or extension mechanism to point at. Placed earlier, the rings would have no register to read, and Belgium would test a definition the reader had not yet seen used.

transition_in.carries_over: The record's lesson that sharing works beneath the product.
transition_in.introduces: A reference architecture for sharing that way.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's reference architecture, not any company's, separates shared from local by layer and puts the tenancy services, on which every layer depends, in the middle.

evidence.what: Figure 3: brands own product surfaces, commercial terms and market policies; the group owns global components and infrastructure; tenancy services carry market differences down as configuration, extensions and release scope.
evidence.shows: Shows where shared and local meet.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Local does not mean outside the platform: local content such as a Polish fee table or a Belgian bilingual form is applied by shared components, so the brand owns the content and the platform owns the mechanism.

transition_in.carries_over: The layered split of shared and local.
transition_in.introduces: What 'local' means in it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The tenant register is the small, authoritative list of tenants that every shared capability reads, and an entry holds the code, brand, country and legal entity, locales, currency, time zone and regulator, hosting and isolation profile, profiles and lifecycle.

evidence.what: BCP 47 tags (RFC 5646, 2009); ISO 4217 codes with minor units; the DSA for statements of reasons.
evidence.shows: Anchors the locale, currency and legal-entity attributes in standards.

transition_in.introduces: Their first element, the register.

transition_in.carries_over: The configuration hierarchy.
transition_in.introduces: A published instance of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four rules keep a configuration hierarchy healthy: every key has a schema, an owner and a level; changes are versioned, reviewed and effective-dated; configuration is data, not logic; and resolution is observable.

transition_in.carries_over: The hierarchy and its published example.
transition_in.introduces: The rules that keep it from decaying.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When configuration is not enough, a shared capability offers extension points, defined interfaces where a tenant-owned component runs under a contract with an owner on each side.

transition_in.carries_over: Configuration and its limit, rule three.
transition_in.introduces: The next rung: extension points.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adevinta's 2023 dispute back office is the clearest published example: per-tenant adapters in, a canonical model in the middle and an extensible surface out, the general pattern for a global component that serves different products.

evidence.what: Events via Kafka, SQS or REST normalized into one model; an extensible micro-frontend; 'We couldn't hardcode anything… or make any assumptions'.
evidence.shows: Shows extension points working in a cross-marketplace component.

transition_in.carries_over: Extension points defined.
transition_in.introduces: A published instance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The configure–extend–fork ladder decides which mechanism a difference gets, with an owner and an exit for each rung.

evidence.what: Configure (a value; brand content on a group schema); extend (behavior at a known point; promote to core if a second tenant needs it); fork (neither works and the market cannot wait; expiry date and a plan to fold back or leave).
evidence.shows: Shows when each rung applies and how each ends.

transition_in.carries_over: Configuration and extension points.
transition_in.introduces: The ladder that chooses between them and the fork.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The fork rung exists because pretending it does not starts shadow systems: a declared, dated fork is a managed exception, an undeclared one the Copy-Paste Country in miniature.

transition_in.carries_over: The fork rung in the ladder.
transition_in.introduces: Why it is there.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Releases of a shared platform are scoped by tenant through release rings, which move a deployment from synthetic to small to the largest tenants, and tenant-scoped feature flags, whose release toggles must expire.

evidence.what: Hodgson's taxonomy of release, experiment, operational and permission toggles.
evidence.shows: Shows why release toggles need an expiry.

transition_in.carries_over: How a difference is expressed: configuration, extension or fork.
transition_in.introduces: How a change reaches each tenant.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Rings limit a defect's blast radius and flags let a tenant adopt a change on its schedule, but some changes must not wait for any schedule, so the tenancy model names group-urgent change classes in advance.

evidence.what: A fraud rule, a security fix or a legal takedown.
evidence.shows: Names the changes that bypass rings.

transition_in.carries_over: Rings and flags as two mechanisms.
transition_in.introduces: Their opposite purposes and the changes that must bypass both.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For an EU group, data residency does not mean keeping data in the user's country: GDPR Chapter V restricts transfers outside the EEA, so EU hosting with governed outside access covers most needs, and stricter constraints go in the register's hosting profile.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Chapter V.
evidence.shows: States the actual legal constraint.

transition_in.carries_over: The mechanisms that express and release a tenant's differences.
transition_in.introduces: What tenants may not share: where their data may live and who may use it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The harder boundary in a multi-brand group is legal and commercial, which tenant may use which data, so a shared platform needs tenant-scoped access by default and explicit, recorded exceptions.

evidence.what: Purpose limitation, competition law, platform-to-business commitments, the group's promises; a shared fraud block list as an exception.
evidence.shows: Shows why data in one warehouse is not free to share.

transition_in.carries_over: The geographic boundary.
transition_in.introduces: The legal and commercial boundary between tenants.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Multi-region deployment is a separate decision that country-scoped classifieds rarely need; Vinted's single cross-border catalog with a primary writer and replicated read projections is the documented exception.

evidence.what: 'not to shard our primary data models across regions'; 'Eventual consistency is being built into how the system works, not an edge case we try to hide'.
evidence.shows: Shows what a truly global dataset demands and why most groups do not need it.

transition_in.carries_over: Boundaries between tenants' data.
transition_in.introduces: Whether data spans regions at all.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Localization in a listing platform touches at least six layers, and only the first is text: interface text, formats, taxonomy labels, search analysis, legal and policy content, and trust content.

evidence.what: Unicode CLDR plural and gender rules; links to location-and-geo, categories-and-taxonomies, attribute-schemas, search-architecture.
evidence.shows: Places each layer with its standard or owning chapter.

transition_in.carries_over: Configuration, extensions and release scope, and the boundaries between tenants.
transition_in.introduces: Language: the market difference that runs through every layer and uses all of those mechanisms.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Belgium is the test case: in 2013 eBay described 2dehands.be and 2ememain.be as one bilingual marketplace under two names, so a model that equates tenant with locale, or brand with domain, cannot represent it.

evidence.what: eBay Classifieds Group brand page, 2013 archived snapshot: 'bilingual' Dutch and French search and listing.
evidence.shows: Shows one tenant, one inventory, two locales and two names.

transition_in.carries_over: Localization beyond translation.
transition_in.introduces: A market that tests the tenant definition.

sections.heading: In Practice: Veldmark's Tenancy Model v1
sections.controlling_idea: Veldmark's Tenancy model v1 of 9 June 2027 applies every element of the reference architecture, and its two tests (the phishing replay and the classification of Yardstick's branches), one market that combines the layers (Polish vehicles) and its first release (the taxonomy service's rings) confirm it and refine it.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the tenancy model decided, tested and used at a group with the scene's problem.

flow.rationale: In date order: the decision record and the arguments it settled (June 2027), the rings' first use for the taxonomy service (October 2027), the replay of the phishing rule before the trust-and-safety platform went live (November 2027), the branch classification for the insertion flow leaving Yardstick (Q2 2028), and the Polish vehicles section, which combines configuration, extensions and commercial ownership and so needs both tests before it. The rings follow the arguments because the second argument was about ring placement; in any other order the dates jump, which both round-2 flow readers reported.

transition_in.carries_over: The reference tenancy model.
transition_in.introduces: Veldmark's decision record that applies it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The decision record adopted on 9 June 2027 had nine parts, from ten brand × country tenants to tenant exit paths, each with its reason.

evidence.what: 1 ten tenant codes; 2 codes in every identifier vm:<brand>:<country>:<id>, event, API call, log line, metric, cache key and cost tag; 3 Keybridge not a tenant; 4 partitioned default; 5 one configuration service, group → brand → tenant → profile → seller segment → experiment; 6 extension points (VIN decoding, energy certificates, Polish insertion fees); 7 release rings; 8 group-urgent classes; 9 tenant exit paths, because a private-equity owner may sell any tenant.
evidence.shows: Shows every element of the reference architecture decided for one group.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two decisions that drew argument were settled by scope and by traffic: the configuration service is mandatory only for global components, so Motorvane keeps its own, and Poland is too large to be a canary.

evidence.what: Felix Brandt's objection; Katarzyna Nowak's question; Poland with 3.6 million live listings and 8.9 million monthly users.
evidence.shows: Shows how the model answers a brand that already solved multi-country and a market that wanted to go early.

transition_in.carries_over: The record as adopted.
transition_in.introduces: The two parts of it that were contested.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The rings were first used for the group taxonomy and attribute service in October 2027, and the ring-1 week found two defects, one of them a cache key without the tenant code, which is why decision 2 requires the code in every cache key.

evidence.what: ty:pt on Monday 4 October 2027, ring 2 a week later, ty:nl on Monday 25 October, a week before the bikes split on 1 November; a Portuguese label falling back to Dutch; a cache key missing the tenant code.
evidence.shows: Shows rings catching the classic multi-tenant bug before the largest tenant.

transition_in.carries_over: The ring placement argued over, Poland too large to be a canary.
transition_in.introduces: The rings' first use, for the taxonomy service in October 2027.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Before the shared trust-and-safety platform went live for Tradeyard Netherlands and Belgium in November 2027, Ingrid's team replayed the 7 March incident against it as a design test of the tenancy model.

evidence.what: Figure 5: the rule as policy content with a tenant scope; tenants in other languages in shadow mode until a locale term list is reviewed.
evidence.shows: Shows the rule's path on the shared platform.

transition_in.carries_over: The rings' first use in October 2027.
transition_in.introduces: The replay of the scene's incident before the shared trust-and-safety platform went live in November 2027.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The replay produced three findings that went back into the model: rules split into a group detector and tenant locale packs, cross-brand signals need one recorded exception, and statements of reasons stay tenant-scoped.

evidence.what: The domain-age signal and link pattern global, the wording Dutch; a 48-hour shadow window for Polish and Portuguese packs; a shared block list of hashed identifiers of accounts terminated for fraud, approved by the Group Data Protection Officer; DSA statements of reasons issued per Member State.
evidence.shows: Shows what the test changed.

transition_in.carries_over: The replay.
transition_in.introduces: What it found.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second test, on the Tradeyard insertion flow leaving Yardstick in Q2 2028, sampled 300 of the 2,600 country branches and found about 70% values, 20% behavior and 10% dead code, and no branch that justified a fork.

evidence.what: Daan Visser's team's sample: about 70% configuration, about 20% extensions (Polish insertion fees, Belgian title language detection, Portuguese tax identifiers), about 10% dead; Figure 6.
evidence.shows: Shows configuration over code removing country branches without a fork.

transition_in.carries_over: The first test, on trust and safety.
transition_in.introduces: The second, on the insertion flow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Polish vehicles section shows the layers combined: one market, two brands, one shared capability and two commercial owners, all of which the tenancy model has to represent.

evidence.what: Private-seller listings in tenant ty:pl, with insertion fees in złoty from the ty:pl vehicles profile; Motorvane's VIN decoding through the same extension contract; dealers offered Motorvane packages in tenant mv:pl and syndicated to Tradeyard; the listing core records the commercial owner.
evidence.shows: Shows configuration, extensions and ownership working together in one market.

transition_in.carries_over: The branch classification.
transition_in.introduces: One market where all mechanisms meet.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.controlling_idea: The platform model and the isolation tier are chosen per capability, and the configure-and-share approach stops holding when a market's product has structurally diverged, one tenant dominates, or ownership is about to change.

advances_thesis.how: Sets out the per-capability choices and states when the thesis does not hold.

transition_in.carries_over: Veldmark's decisions and their tests.
transition_in.introduces: The choices behind them, set side by side, and their limits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's tested decisions rest on choices every group faces, so the section sets them side by side in two tables (a platform model per capability, an isolation tier per workload) and then says when the guidance does not hold.

Read across the two trade-off tables, a capability with uniform technology goes to a global component on a partitioned default while the brand keeps its insertion flow, web, apps and prices, and Veldmark's 2027 choices follow that line.

evidence.what: Platform model per capability with Veldmark's 2027 choice (compute, identity, trust and safety, search, taxonomy, catalog, insertion flow, web and apps, packages and prices).
evidence.shows: Shows the per-capability decision and Veldmark's choices.

evidence.what: Isolation choices: logical everywhere, partitioned by default, dedicated for the largest tenant, dedicated per tenant, with benefit, cost and when each is right.
evidence.shows: Shows partitioned as the default and when each alternative wins.

transition_in.carries_over: The two tables the lead-in announced.
transition_in.introduces: What they show read together, and Veldmark's choices along that line.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The configure-and-share approach fails when a market's product has diverged for structural reasons, when one tenant is so large that the shared platform becomes its platform, and when ownership is likely to change soon.

evidence.what: A transactional model among lead-based ones; a regulatory regime with no equivalent; a dominant tenant; an imminent sale (case-adevinta).
evidence.shows: Names the conditions under which the guidance does not hold.

transition_in.carries_over: The choices the tables recommend.
transition_in.introduces: When those choices do not hold.

sections.heading: Vertical Differences
sections.controlling_idea: Every vertical shares its engines and identity easily and its country-specific edges hardly at all, and real estate is the hardest vertical to share across countries.

advances_thesis.how: Shows where sharing beneath the product stops in each vertical.

transition_in.carries_over: The trade-offs and the conditions under which sharing stops holding.
transition_in.introduces: How those limits fall in each vertical, which the section's opening sentence names.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Real estate is the hardest vertical to share across countries, because professional-software ecosystems, mandatory disclosures and valuation data differ most there, so a shared engine with local ingestion, disclosure and pro-tooling edges fits the evidence and a single property product does not.

evidence.what: What varies by country, what is easiest and hardest to share, and the documented signal, for general classifieds, real estate, automotive and jobs.
evidence.shows: Shows the same split, shared engines and local edges, in every vertical.

sections.heading: Failure Modes
sections.controlling_idea: Eight failure modes recur when the tenancy model is missing or partial, from the tenant added as an afterthought to the missing exit path.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the cost of omitting each element of the tenancy model.

transition_in.carries_over: Where sharing fits each vertical.
transition_in.introduces: What goes wrong when the tenancy model is missing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eight failure modes recur: the tenant added as an afterthought, brand equated with domain or locale, configuration that became code, release toggles that never expire, rings without a group-urgent lane, the largest tenant as design authority, pooled data without recorded boundaries, and no exit path.

evidence.what: Belgium, Poland's vehicles section and a rebrand break brand-as-domain; Tradeyard Netherlands carries about 45% of Tradeyard's search traffic; Keybridge's commitments.
evidence.shows: Ties several failures to the chapter's cases.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: A Chief Architect decides the tenancy model once at group level, the platform model per capability, what to share first and who decides what, watches six measures, and designs the platform to survive the next swing of the centralization pendulum.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the thesis into decisions, an order of sharing and measures.

flow.rationale: The group-level tenancy decision comes first because everything else may vary by capability; then the per-capability model, the sharing order that follows from it, the split of decision rights, the measures that show whether it works, and last the pendulum, which explains why all of it is designed to be reversible. Placed before the per-capability scoring, the sharing order would have no criteria behind it; placed first, the pendulum would argue for reversibility before the reader knows what is being shared.

transition_in.carries_over: The failure modes.
transition_in.introduces: The decisions that prevent them at group scale.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Decide the tenancy model once, early, at group level: the tenant definition, code format, mandatory carriage and exit-path requirement are the only parts that may not vary by capability.

Decide the platform model per capability by asking whether it passes both halves of Adevinta's 2019 test, whether its value grows when data is pooled, and whether it can be shared without converging the product above it, and publish the scores.

transition_in.carries_over: What is decided once for the group.
transition_in.introduces: What is decided per capability.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Share in order infrastructure and cloud governance, the event backbone and data platform, trust signals and identity, media and the search engine, then taxonomy and the catalog and entitlements model, with product surfaces last and often never.

evidence.what: Uniform and invisible; everything depends on them; value grows with pooling and fraud ignores brand boundaries; expensive and uniform; need the tenancy services first.
evidence.shows: Gives the reason for each step; platform-consolidation develops the post-acquisition variant.

transition_in.carries_over: The three questions for scoring a capability.
transition_in.introduces: The order of sharing they produce.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The group decides schemas, contracts and the tenancy model, the brand decides configuration values, extensions and product, the platform team decides how a capability is built and run, and the forum decides forks, with an expiry date.

transition_in.carries_over: What to share and in what order.
transition_in.introduces: Who decides what.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Six measures show whether the model works: adoption without mandate, country branches in code, configuration health, lead time from one tenant to all, cost per tenant, and yearly separability drills.

evidence.what: On 7 March 2027 the lead time was three days to Belgium and never to Poland or Portugal.
evidence.shows: Gives the measure a baseline from the scene.

transition_in.carries_over: Decision rights.
transition_in.introduces: The measures that show whether the decisions work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Groups swing between centralization and local autonomy faster than platforms change, so the goal is not the right position on the pendulum but a platform that survives the next swing.

evidence.what: Adevinta (2023 convergence, 2025 decentralization) and AVIV (2021 integration, 2025 localization).
evidence.shows: Shows the pendulum swinging within a few years at both public examples.

evidence.what: Global components a tenant can leave, configuration it can take with it, products that never depended on another brand's code; long-term-evolution's cost to reverse.
evidence.shows: Shows how the architecture makes the swing cheap.

transition_in.carries_over: The measures, including separability drills.
transition_in.introduces: Why reversibility is the design goal.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask
sections.controlling_idea: Ten questions let an architect test a group's platform against the tenancy model: tenant codes, isolation, branches in code, configuration governance, extension points, lead time to all tenants, shared data, exit paths, adoption without mandate and convergence initiatives.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the reader a working review drawn from every section.

transition_in.carries_over: The Chief Architect's decisions and measures.
transition_in.introduces: Questions that test whether they are in place.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten questions test whether a group's tenant codes, isolation tiers, branches in code, configuration governance, extension points, lead time to all tenants, shared data, exit paths, adoption and convergence initiatives meet the chapter's design.

conclusion.heading: From Sharing to Staying Up
conclusion.synthesis: Each kind of market difference has one place to live (a value in configuration at its level, a behavior in an extension point, a fork only under an expiry date, an urgent rule in a group-urgent lane), and all of them depend on one thing decided once: a tenant code carried everywhere, with an exit path for every tenant.
conclusion.so_what: With that model each fraud rule, search upgrade or consent change is built once and reaches every tenant, while each market keeps what makes it local and the group can still sell or move a tenant.

callback.to: The scene's 7 March phishing rule, which reached Belgium three days late and Poland and Portugal never, and Ingrid's question of where each difference should live.
callback.how: The conclusion answers Ingrid's question difference by difference and shows the replayed rule reaching every tenant at once, with locale packs following within the shadow window.

takeaway.content: Write the tenancy decision record first: tenant definition and codes, mandatory carriage, isolation default, configuration hierarchy, rings with group-urgent classes, and an exit path per capability.

hand_off.carries_over: A tenancy model decides how the platform is shared, but not whether the shared platform stays up when every tenant uses it at once.

evidence.what: The 7 March rule; Belgium on 10 March; Poland and Portugal never; the replay's detector and locale packs within the 48-hour shadow window.
